 - Meteorological Overview:

A complex evolution to the upper level pattern will continue 
through today, initially with a large upper level trough with 
multiple embedded vort maxes sinking southward from the Pacific 
Northwest, elongating as it does so. At the surface an area of low
pressure centered in North Dakota has pulled a cold front 
southward across the plains early this morning. The combination of
this front, favorable forcing, and ample moisture has resulted in
a round of precipitation developing across much of North Central 
and Central Montana. Precipitation in the form of rain across 
many areas will continue to transition to snow as cold air 
advection near the surface wins out. A precipitation transitions
to snow expect the snow characteristic to be of the wet and heavy
variety, especially at lower elevations, which raises concern for
trees with leaves on them still seeing snapped branches, 
potentially impacting power lines. - AM/Moldan

Colder air continues to sink southward into Southwest Montana 
heading into Sunday, though there remains some uncertainty with 
respect to just how far it makes it. Aloft the complex evolution 
continues, with the upper level troughing elongating further, while 
also interacting with the remnants of Rachel as they lift 
northeastward ahead of the trough axis. Ample moisture associated 
with not only the main troughing, but the remnants of Rachel will 
support the expansion of precipitation southward into Southwest 
Montana during the day Sunday as an upper level jet moves overhead.
The extent of impactful snowfall across Southwest Montana will 
follow where the coldest air both aloft and at the surface ends up
settling. Banded precipitation looks to persists into Monday 
morning across portions of Central and Southwest Montana before 
subsiding through the day. 

The region looks to dry out for at least a couple days as the upper 
level troughing consolidates once again across the desert Southwest. 
Uncertainty grows a bit toward Thursday, though the majority of 
ensemble members remain dry Thursday toward the weekend. -AM

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

Snowfall through Sunday night/Monday morning...

Overall confidence in snowfall amounts continues to increase for 
areas north of the US Hwy 12 corridor, along/near the Montana Hwy 
200 corridor, and west of the US Hwy 89 corridor across Central and 
portions of North Central Montana. Here Hi-Res guidance has been 
consistently showing a nearly stationary band of moderate to heavy 
snow through much of the next 48 hours, with additional orographic 
enhancement from the mid-slopes of the Little Belts and Rocky 
Mountain Front out onto the adjacent plains above 3500 feet. 

As has been the case from previous forecasts snowfall amounts will 
vary drastically from grassy/elevated surfaces to roadways/paved 
surfaces given relatively warm ground temperatures and the effects 
of a higher October sun angle (during the daylight hours) as 
compared to the heart of the winter season. With that being said, 
surface temperatures along and west of the I-15 corridor over the 
plains of Central and North Central Montana have already fallen into 
the mid- to upper 30s, which will be favorable for snowfall to 
accumulate on roadways in these areas by the late afternoon hours 
today as solar insolation decreases. Along with the impacts to 
travel to the region the heavy, wet nature of the snow has the 
potential to cause considerable tree damage where foliage still 
remains. Additionally, this heavy, wet snow accumulating on 
powerlines and breezy north winds could result in isolated power 
outages.

Current suite of winter weather statement remain valid outside of 
the East Glacier Park Region and Northern High Plains where the 
Winter Weather Advisory has been upgraded to a Winter Storm Warning 
due to a trend in higher snowfall amounts. Additional focus was 
given to areas south and east of a Bozeman to Dillon, and the Helena 
Valley for the potential need to upgrade the current advisories to 
warnings. Ultimately concerns about snow levels and/or marginal 
surface temperatures still remain and confidence in warning level 
amounts/impacts remain too low for an upgrade.

Low Temperatures Monday night/Tuesday morning...

Clearing skies, light winds, and a relatively fresh snowpack will 
likely result in the coldest temperatures of the upcoming week, with 
a 25% chance that lows fall into the teens across Southwest through 
North Central Montana. Model guidance is notorious for 
under-performing with respect to low temperatures given the 
aforementioned conditions, so it is reasonable to believe that lows 
could fall as low as the single digits above zero at some locations 
during the timeframe. - Moldan
